Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Monroe: Alright hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the account lead. We also have Priya from solutions engineering. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Lena Park: Hey Alex, doing good thanks. Marcus and Diane are on. We'll just jump in, we have a tight window so appreciate that.
[00:14] Marcus Velez: Yep thanks, excited to go through this.
[00:18] Priya Rao: Great, quick agenda, we'll run through a few questions about your workloads, traffic shape, isolation needs, then we can map that to reserved GPU options and burst/warmpool patterns. Sound good?
[00:29] Lena Park: Sounds good. I can start with context: we've got an inference platform that powers a real-time genomics annotation API. 99th percentile latency goal is around 180ms for short requests but typical token lengths are small, mostly classification-ish prompts. We do see spiky bursts during batch ingest windows.
[00:49] Marcus Velez: To add, current setup is a mix of hosted endpoints on CloudGiant for dev and an internal Kubernetes cluster with models on commodity GPUs for some heavy offline steps. We're looking for something more predictable for production inference.
[01:08] Diane Chu: Security overview from our side: we need customer-managed keys for certain datasets, audit logs for requests, and evidence of SOC2 or similar. Also data residency is a possibility for EU-only subsets.
[01:26] Alex Monroe: Okay, useful. Quick clarifying question — when you say bursts, what's the multiplier versus baseline and are bursts short spikes or multi-hour sustained windows?
[01:36] Lena Park: It's a mix. Baseline is low — maybe 30 qps — but during a nightly analysis job around 02:00 UTC we spike to 900 qps for about 20-45 minutes. We also get smaller spikes like 200-300 qps during daytime releases.
[01:52] Priya Rao: Got it. That pattern argues for reserved capacity with a burst policy and warm pool pre-warmed nodes. You can reserve a base pool to cover baseline and then allow burst to either dedicated warm nodes or fallback to hosted for overflow.
[02:07] Marcus Velez: Two practical constraints: we need strict tenant isolation for clinical customers and per-tenant rate shaping. Also, preemption of other jobs on our infra causes jitter — we want predictable latency.
[02:21] Alex Monroe: Right, so dedicated reserved nodes with tenant fencing looks like the natural fit. We support VPC peering and a Private deployment if you need on-prem. For the hosted dedicated option we can provide dedicated GPU pools in your VPC for most clouds — and provide committed capacity with burstable hotpool.
[02:39] Lena Park: What's the tradeoff on cost though? We don't want to massively overcommit.
[02:44] Priya Rao: Good question. There are two levers: how many GPUs you reserve (committed cost) and how you configure warm pools and burst fallback. Warm pool carries cost but reduces cold-start latency and satisfies short spikes. Fallback to hosted on overflow avoids overcommit but increases per-token cost and higher tail latency.
[03:05] Alex Monroe: To give a concrete example, if you reserve N 80GB A100 equivalent nodes to cover baseline, you'd pay the committed rate. If your spike is 900 qps and baseline only covers 100 qps, you'd either provision a warmpool sized to cover the delta, or accept fallback overflow, or a hybrid: smaller warmpool + hosted overflow.
[03:26] Marcus Velez: For the warmpool, is that per-tenant or shared across tenants? We need tenant-level isolation for regulated clients.
[03:33] Priya Rao: We offer both patterns. For regulated tenants you can pin dedicated nodes to that tenant (hard isolation). For multi-tenant customers you can use hotpool with soft isolation and per-tenant quotas. Pinning increases committed footprint but guarantees compute isolation.
[03:49] Diane Chu: Re: KMS, does Redwood support customer-managed keys and HSM-backed KMS?
[03:54] Alex Monroe: Yes, we integrate with cloud KMS and can support customer-owned keys in most enterprise setups; for Private on-prem bundles we can integrate with HSMs as well. We'll share our encryption/KMS FAQ in the follow-up — I can put that in the next-steps.
[04:06] Lena Park: Good. On the eviction model — if our warmpool nodes get preempted for infra reasons, how fast can you failover and what happens to KV cache? We rely on KV cache heavily for burst latency.
[04:18] Priya Rao: We manage KV cache differently depending on topology. For dedicated pinned nodes the KV cache stays local to that instance. Warmpool eviction means cache is lost and requests hitting a cold node may see a latency penalty for the first few tokens. We mitigate with quick fallback to hosted or replicate KV snapshots to standby nodes for critical tenants — but that is an architectural tradeoff.
[04:38] Marcus Velez: Replicating KV snapshots sounds heavy, but might be necessary for clinical latency SLAs. What about prewarming strategies? Do you have options for model residency vs transfer costs?
[04:48] Priya Rao: Yep — we have prewarming where a model is kept resident in GPU memory in the warmpool. There's an option for a 'sticky warmpool' where models are kept hot for longer at a cost, versus ephemeral prewarm that pulls weights on demand. Transfer cost is usually network + local copy time; for large models quantization can help reduce residency size and transfer time.
[05:06] Lena Park: We're using a custom 8B variant with some fine-tuning; quantization is a possibility but we need to validate quality first. Any guidance on supported quant formats?
[05:14] Priya Rao: We support 8-bit and mixed quant strategies and can provide recommendations after seeing your eval prompts. Redwood Optimize can run a quick suggestion profile. We'll run a small eval during the benchmark run.
[05:27] Alex Monroe: Quick practical: what metrics would you use to decide committed sizing? QPS, concurrent requests, per-request token count?
[05:36] Marcus Velez: For us it's peak concurrency and 99p latency. Token count is small, but concurrency during those windows is the problem. The nightly job is mostly synchronous calls with low tokens but high throughput.
[05:48] Priya Rao: Then we'd size on concurrent model instances and expected serving throughput per GPU. We'll also ask for workload traces so we can map to an expected GPU RPS. Please send the 7-day trace as a CSV and we'll run a modeling exercise.
[06:02] Lena Park: Will do. Also curious about SLA for dedicated pools — uptime and tail latency guarantees?
[06:10] Alex Monroe: For Dedicated we offer an SLA that covers availability of the reserved pool and committed capacity. Tail latency is part of our SLO conversation; we provide latency SLOs for specific configs and can agree in the contract. The hosted fallback path includes different SLOs with higher tail latency.
[06:27] Diane Chu: On audit logs: we need request-level metadata for compliance, but we also have PII concerns. How are logs masked and retained?
[06:36] Priya Rao: We provide configurable logging retention and redaction options. For PII-sensitive datasets you can disable full logs and capture only metadata, or redact request bodies before storage. We can provide examples of the audit log schema.
[06:48] Marcus Velez: What about traffic shaping? We want per-tenant shaping and emergency throttles during storms.
[06:55] Alex Monroe: We have per-tenant quotas, dynamic rate shaping and emergency circuit-breakers that can route overflow to hosted or reject based on policy. Those policies are plumbed through the console and API.
[07:08] Lena Park: Ok this is helpful. On the procurement side we probably need an initial 6-month commit then re-evaluate after 3 months based on actual usage. Is there flexibility on initial commit?
[07:19] Alex Monroe: Yes we have standard 6- and 12-month contracts; we can do a ramped commit with a lower initial guaranteed and defined uplift windows. We also offer trial credits and a benchmark run to validate performance before full commit.
[07:33] Diane Chu: One more question — do you support private deployments in our VPC with no egress to Redwood control plane for certain datasets?
[07:41] Priya Rao: We offer Private deployments where the control plane can be customer‑managed. There are variants: managed VPC with peering and private endpoints, or fully on-prem air-gapped bundles for regulated workloads. We'll list the options in a follow-up doc.
[07:56] Marcus Velez: For the benchmark run, what do you need from us?
[07:59] Priya Rao: Sample model artifact or a containerized model, a representative request trace, and keys for any private registry access. We'll run a 1–2 hour simulated burst that matches your nightly pattern.
[08:10] Alex Monroe: Great. Quick recap for next steps: I'll send pricing and commitment options; Priya will share dedicated topology diagram, warmpool notes, and the audit-log schema. You'll send traffic traces and decide on a target pilot window. We'll schedule the benchmark for week of 2025-10-27.
[08:29] Lena Park: Sounds good. Any blockers on our side? Diane: you comfortable with that timeline?
[08:35] Diane Chu: Yes, we'll aim to get the traces and the compliance checklist to you by the end of next week.
[08:40] Alex Monroe: Perfect. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and I'll include the security docs and pricing.
[08:46] Lena Park: Thanks guys. Bye.
[08:48] Marcus Velez: Bye.
